title: Why does mathematics ask why the Sun rises?
description: The Sun rises every day, and noticing it only gives a list of mornings. The video shows that a reason gives a rule which can be used in other places, such as in launching satellites, and Keeko's doubt, that noticing is enough, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: mathematics looks for the reason behind a pattern, because a reason gives a rule that works elsewhere. Watch for students who think noticing a pattern is all that mathematics does.

source: The Sun rises every day. Why does mathematics not stop at no
video_script.why: The child sees that mathematics searches for the explanation of a pattern too, because an explanation can be used well beyond where it was found.
video_script.substitution: A list of mornings is only noticing; a reason for the motion of the Sun is a rule.
video_script.anchor: the Sun and the Moon moving across the sky, then a satellite and a rocket going up
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says noticing is enough, because the Sun will rise tomorrow anyway. A list of mornings cannot say what happens in a place nobody has watched, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The reason gives a rule that can be used elsewhere

final_answer.value: the reason gives a rule that can be used elsewhere
final_answer.spoken: the reason gives a rule that can be used elsewhere, which a list of what happened cannot

hold_back: The reason gives a rule that can be used elsewhere
maths_rules: noticing: the Sun comes back every day, which is only a list of what happened
explaining: mathematics looks for a rule for the motion of the Sun, the Moon and the night sky
the book: understanding such patterns led to the theory of gravitation, which lets us launch satellites and send rockets to the Moon and to Mars
a rule found in one place can be used in other places
video_script.design: One idea: a reason gives a rule that works elsewhere. Assumes the idea of a pattern. Wrong idea: noticing is enough. The Sun stays on the board to the end.
